articles.title: Sudan’s farmers are ready to return – private investment could get them there
articles.summary: The war in Sudan has devastated the economy and agricultural production, but a UN-backed plan aims to mobilise private sector investment to help farmers return to their fields.
articles.content:
The roadmap for recovery, and the potential for some $155 million in external investment, were among the outcomes of a three-day dialogue held this week in Khartoum, organized by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) and Sudan’s Ministry of Finance.

More than 300 participants from 20 countries – representing the Government, financial institutions, the national and international private sector, farmers’ and trade associations, as well as other stakeholders – registered for the event.

A ‘stepping stone’ forward

“This dialogue is a stepping stone towards moving forward in bringing more private sector engagement, which ultimately socioeconomic recovery depends on,” said Arvind Kumar, Team Leader for Recovery and Resilience at the UNDP Country Office in Sudan.

Tweet URL

He told UN News that focusing on the private sector is critical because it provides some 98 per cent of jobs.

Speaking from the capital, Mr. Kumar described an economy that has been broken by war but not completely paralysed. Sudan’s farmers continue to grow crops, goods are still being transported, and markets still function in some areas.

But the last two years have seen yields fall by 40 to 70 per cent in some cases, he said, while the cost of agricultural inputs such as fertilisers and fuel have increased due to the crisis in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf.

“The third and most key important aspect is that there is not much injection into the economy from the private sector,” he said. “And they are willing to come back.”

Millions going hungry

Mr. Kumar stressed that “food production is obviously not close to what Sudan needs,” highlighting the immense impacts of the civil war that erupted in April 2023.

The brutal battle between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has left more than 19 million people facing hunger. Nearly 35 million require humanitarian assistance and 13 million have been displaced.

Before the war, Sudan exported gum arabic, sesame, cotton, hibiscus, sorghum and livestock, he said, and once accounted for a 12 to 13 per cent share of the global sesame market, now reduced to six per cent.

Although livestock exports continue, the share of “high-value agricultural crops” has declined because most businesses have lost assets and lack access to capital, “therefore it is very difficult for them to come and rebuild, so it is taking time.”

Meanwhile, UNDP analysis shows that 90 per cent of farmers cannot access financing, and “with the support only of aid, they will not be able to continue to improve food production.”

Recognition, recovery and potential resources

He said the dialogue in Khartoum concluded with “three key outcomes”: recognition of the need for continued engagement with the international and national private sector, adoption and endorsement of a private sector recovery roadmap for agriculture, and “an encouraging potential investment” of nearly $155 million from Pakistan, India, Türkiye, Egypt and Syria.

Participants also discussed the need to re-connect farms with markets and ultimately buyers, while business owners raised concerns about regulatory barriers and the difficulty of linking up with international investors.

Financial support for farmers

UNDP is exploring measures to bring more support to farmers through the banking system, such as credit guarantees.

It is also working with the national and international private sector to restore a warehouse receipt system – a process that would allow farmers to store produce in approved facilities and receive receipts that may be used to secure financing.

Trade facilitation is another top priority. UNDP is engaging with the Sudanese authorities responsible for customs and ports, as well as UN trade and development organization UNCTAD, “to review the reforms that are needed for ease of business.”

Mr. Kumar said people need education, healthcare, electricity and jobs to rebuild their lives, He insisted that development should begin alongside life-saving humanitarian assistance “and there is an opportunity and a space to bring development back on track.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant UN-backed initiative to mobilize private sector investment to help Sudanese farmers recover from the devastating impacts of war. This plan has broad socioeconomic implications for millions affected by hunger and displacement, focusing on agricultural recovery, market reconnection, and financial support. The story provides substantial context about the challenges and concrete steps being taken, representing a meaningful positive development for Sudan's recovery and food security.
articles.personality_title: UN plan aims to help Sudanese farmers recover with private investment
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Sudan’s war has caused severe damage to its economy and farming. Many farmers have stopped working, and food production has dropped a lot. Millions of people now struggle with hunger and need help.

**What happened** – A three-day meeting in Khartoum, led by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Sudan’s Ministry of Finance, brought together over 300 participants from 20 countries. They discussed ways to encourage private companies to invest nearly $155 million to support farmers and rebuild agriculture.

**Impact** – This plan is important because private businesses provide almost all jobs in Sudan. Even though the war has hurt farming, some farmers still grow crops, and markets keep working in parts of the country. The new investment could help farmers buy seeds, fertilisers, and fuel, and connect them better to markets. Without private investment, farmers cannot get the money they need to grow enough food.

**What's next step** – UNDP will work with banks to offer loans and create systems that let farmers store their crops safely and use them to get financing. They will also help improve trade rules to make it easier for farmers to sell their products. These efforts aim to bring back jobs and improve life for many Sudanese people.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new UN-backed plan is set to boost Sudan’s farming by attracting private investment, helping farmers return to work and improving food supply in the country.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un plan de l’ONU pour aider les agriculteurs soudanais grâce à l’investissement privé
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La guerre au Soudan a gravement endommagé son économie et l’agriculture. Beaucoup d’agriculteurs ont cessé de travailler et la production alimentaire a fortement chuté. Des millions de personnes souffrent de la faim et ont besoin d’aide.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une réunion de trois jours à Khartoum, organisée par le Programme des Nations Unies pour le développement (PNUD) et le ministère soudanais des Finances, a rassemblé plus de 300 participants de 20 pays. Ils ont discuté des moyens d’encourager les entreprises privées à investir près de 155 millions de dollars pour soutenir les agriculteurs et reconstruire l’agriculture.

**Impact** – Ce plan est important car les entreprises privées fournissent presque tous les emplois au Soudan. Même si la guerre a affecté l’agriculture, certains agriculteurs continuent de cultiver et les marchés fonctionnent encore dans certaines régions. Ce nouvel investissement pourrait aider les agriculteurs à acheter des graines, des engrais et du carburant, et à mieux se connecter aux marchés. Sans investissement privé, les agriculteurs ne peuvent pas obtenir l’argent nécessaire pour produire suffisamment de nourriture.

**Prochaine étape** – Le PNUD travaillera avec les banques pour offrir des prêts et créer des systèmes permettant aux agriculteurs de stocker leurs récoltes en toute sécurité et de les utiliser pour obtenir des financements. Il aidera aussi à améliorer les règles commerciales pour faciliter la vente des produits agricoles. Ces efforts visent à créer des emplois et améliorer la vie de nombreux Soudanais.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un nouveau plan soutenu par l’ONU vise à relancer l’agriculture soudanaise en attirant des investissements privés, aidant les agriculteurs à reprendre leur activité et à améliorer l’approvisionnement alimentaire dans le pays.
articles.personality_title_es: Plan de la ONU busca ayudar a agricultores sudaneses con inversión privada
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La guerra en Sudán ha dañado gravemente su economía y agricultura. Muchos agricultores dejaron de trabajar y la producción de alimentos cayó mucho. Millones de personas enfrentan hambre y necesitan ayuda.

**Qué pasó** – En Jartum, una reunión de tres días organizada por el Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo (PNUD) y el Ministerio de Finanzas de Sudán reunió a más de 300 participantes de 20 países. Discutieron cómo motivar a empresas privadas a invertir cerca de 155 millones de dólares para apoyar a los agricultores y reconstruir la agricultura.

**Impacto** – Este plan es importante porque el sector privado genera casi todos los empleos en Sudán. Aunque la guerra dañó la agricultura, algunos agricultores siguen cultivando y los mercados funcionan en ciertas zonas. La nueva inversión podría ayudar a comprar semillas, fertilizantes y combustible, y conectar mejor a los agricultores con los mercados. Sin inversión privada, los agricultores no pueden obtener el dinero necesario para producir suficiente comida.

**Próximo paso** – El PNUD trabajará con bancos para ofrecer préstamos y crear sistemas que permitan a los agricultores almacenar sus cosechas de forma segura y usar esos productos para obtener financiamiento. También ayudará a mejorar las reglas comerciales para facilitar la venta de productos. Estas acciones buscan devolver empleos y mejorar la vida de muchos sudaneses.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un nuevo plan apoyado por la ONU busca impulsar la agricultura en Sudán mediante inversión privada, ayudando a los agricultores a regresar al trabajo y mejorando el suministro de alimentos en el país.

articles.title: ‘Invest with Iraq’: PM sets out vision for new economic future
articles.summary: Iraq’s Prime Minister, Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, said his country aims to exert its influence as an active economic power in the region, and as a bridge for dialogue and cooperation between its peoples.
articles.content:
He was speaking during the debate of the UN General Assembly’s high-level segment, where he set out his country’s vision for economic growth, stability, and regional cooperation.

“We are moving forward to ensure that the State alone holds decision-making power over war and peace, and that weapons and instruments of power remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions, so that the law is the arbiter and the national interest is the compass,” he said.

He explained that the executive measures being taken in this area are moving in the right direction, as they form the basis for building a State of institutions, protecting sovereignty, consolidating stability and creating the environment needed for development and investment.

With the mission of the international coalition in Iraq now over, he said, “we are moving our relationship with our strategic partners into a new phase, from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation that serves our shared interests.”

He called on everyone to secure borders, address gaps and remain constantly vigilant to prevent an environment conducive to extremism from taking hold.

Energy and development

Mr. Al-Zaidi spoke about institutional reform, saying: “Our Government is waging a battle against corruption and the protection of public funds, and we are pursuing sustainable, substantive reforms to raise the efficiency of performance and improve services.”

He said Iraq is working to draw on successful expertise and innovative practices from the world of economics, finance and business to advance its economic and financial reform, and to provide a secure environment for domestic and foreign investment.

“Our ambition is for Iraq to become a global hub for energy production, and to make use of its capabilities to sustainably strengthen regional and international security and stability,” he said.

But he added: “We view with concern the repercussions linked to freedom of transport and maritime navigation, and the crisis they have caused in the form of rising energy prices worldwide.”

To contain these risks, he said, Iraq is working to diversify its oil export outlets and to develop energy lines and corridors linking the country with Türkiye, Jordan and Syria, reaching on to global markets.

He spoke of the Development Road project as Iraq’s comprehensive vision for regional integration and stability, describing it as an important gateway and strategic corridor for trade, investment, industry and energy, linking east and west from the Grand Faw Port, through Türkiye, to Europe.

“From the podium of the United Nations, we say to the world: invest with Iraq, for it has the resources, the market, the location and the will to build a new economy,” he said.

From conflict to integration

Mr. Al-Zaidi stressed that his country’s vision rests on helping to move the region from conflict to integration, from rivalry to cooperation, and from depleting resources to investing them in development.

He said Iraq reaffirms its support for dialogue and diplomacy to defuse crises, and for efforts to allow trade to pass through Iraqi territory, offering major facilities as alternatives to complex trade routes.

He pointed to the challenges posed by desertification and water scarcity facing Iraq, which affect its food security.

“We affirm our commitment to our legitimate and fair water rights, and we call for the shared management of water resources based on the principles of cooperation and international law,” he said.

He concluded: “Iraq has never been on the margins. It is the heart of history and the pulse of the present, and it is worthy of partnership for the future.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports on Iraq's Prime Minister outlining a comprehensive vision for economic growth, regional cooperation, institutional reform, and stability, which has broad positive implications for the region and global economic integration. It highlights efforts to move from conflict to cooperation, fight corruption, and develop infrastructure and energy corridors, all of which represent meaningful progress with tangible benefits for many people.
articles.personality_title: Iraq's Prime Minister unveils plan for economic growth and regional cooperation
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Iraq has faced years of conflict and instability, but now its Prime Minister, Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, is sharing a new plan to build a stronger economy and better cooperation with neighboring countries.

**What happened** – At the United Nations General Assembly, Mr. Al-Zaidi explained Iraq’s vision for the future. He said the country wants to control its own decisions about war and peace, fight corruption, and improve government services. He also spoke about turning military partnerships into economic ones and creating new trade routes through Iraq.

**Impact** – This plan is important because it aims to bring peace and stability to Iraq and the region. By focusing on energy production, fighting corruption, and building trade connections with countries like Türkiye, Jordan, and Syria, Iraq hopes to become a key player in global markets. It also offers new opportunities for investment and job creation.

**What's next step** – Iraq will work on building energy corridors and trade routes, including the Development Road project, which links the Middle East to Europe. The government will continue reforms to improve services and attract investors. Iraq also plans to address environmental challenges like water shortages by cooperating with neighboring countries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Iraq’s Prime Minister is leading a new effort to transform the country into a stable, cooperative economic hub in the region, inviting the world to invest in its future.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le Premier ministre irakien présente un plan pour la croissance économique et la coopération régionale
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Irak a connu des années de conflits et d’instabilité, mais son Premier ministre, Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, partage désormais un nouveau plan pour construire une économie plus forte et une meilleure coopération avec les pays voisins.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Lors de l’Assemblée générale des Nations Unies, M. Al-Zaidi a expliqué la vision de l’Irak pour l’avenir. Il a déclaré que le pays souhaite contrôler ses propres décisions concernant la guerre et la paix, lutter contre la corruption et améliorer les services publics. Il a aussi évoqué la transformation des partenariats militaires en partenariats économiques et la création de nouvelles routes commerciales à travers l’Irak.

**Impact** – Ce plan est important car il vise à apporter la paix et la stabilité à l’Irak et à la région. En se concentrant sur la production d’énergie, la lutte contre la corruption et la construction de liens commerciaux avec des pays comme la Turquie, la Jordanie et la Syrie, l’Irak espère devenir un acteur clé sur les marchés mondiaux. Cela offre aussi de nouvelles opportunités d’investissement et de création d’emplois.

**Prochaine étape** – L’Irak va travailler à la construction de corridors énergétiques et de routes commerciales, notamment le projet Development Road qui relie le Moyen-Orient à l’Europe. Le gouvernement poursuivra les réformes pour améliorer les services et attirer les investisseurs. L’Irak prévoit aussi de relever les défis environnementaux comme la pénurie d’eau en coopérant avec les pays voisins.

**Phrase clé** – Le Premier ministre irakien mène un nouvel effort pour transformer le pays en un centre économique stable et coopératif dans la région, invitant le monde à investir dans son avenir.
articles.personality_title_es: El primer ministro de Irak presenta un plan para el crecimiento económico y la cooperación regional
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Irak ha vivido años de conflicto e inestabilidad, pero ahora su primer ministro, Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, comparte un nuevo plan para construir una economía más fuerte y mejorar la cooperación con los países vecinos.

**Qué sucedió** – En la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas, el Sr. Al-Zaidi explicó la visión de Irak para el futuro. Dijo que el país quiere controlar sus propias decisiones sobre la guerra y la paz, luchar contra la corrupción y mejorar los servicios públicos. También habló de transformar las alianzas militares en económicas y crear nuevas rutas comerciales a través de Irak.

**Impacto** – Este plan es importante porque busca traer paz y estabilidad a Irak y a la región. Al enfocarse en la producción de energía, la lucha contra la corrupción y la construcción de conexiones comerciales con países como Turquía, Jordania y Siria, Irak espera convertirse en un actor clave en los mercados globales. También ofrece nuevas oportunidades de inversión y empleo.

**Próximo paso** – Irak trabajará en la construcción de corredores energéticos y rutas comerciales, incluido el proyecto Development Road, que conecta Oriente Medio con Europa. El gobierno continuará con reformas para mejorar los servicios y atraer inversores. Irak también planea abordar desafíos ambientales como la escasez de agua cooperando con sus vecinos.

**Frase clave** – El primer ministro de Irak lidera un nuevo esfuerzo para transformar el país en un centro económico estable y cooperativo en la región, invitando al mundo a invertir en su futuro.
